name: Crystagen

card.summary: A Russian three-amino-acid 'bioregulator' peptide with spleen and immune claims backed only by small lab reports.
card.note: No human trials found; research-peptide status.

quick.overview:
Crystagen is a tripeptide from the Khavinson family of short peptide bioregulators, discussed in a Russian paper as an immune-supporting peptide for the ageing spleen.

The literature is small and mostly from the developing group. No human trial exists, and it has no documented role in appearance.
quick.mechanism: The cited paper reports that it activates B-cells in the spleen of ageing animals, alongside related peptides that act on T-helpers.
quick.risks: No safety data in humans was found. It is sold as a research peptide rather than an approved medicine in the sources reviewed.

lead: Crystagen is a synthetic tripeptide of threonine, lysine and glutamic acid, one of the short peptide bioregulators associated with Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia. It is discussed in longevity and anti-ageing circles as an immune-supporting peptide, and the looks interest is the broader promise of healthier ageing, since immune and tissue upkeep are part of how people hope to keep a youthful appearance.[1][2]

The one published paper on it reports that Vilon, Timogen, Crystagen and R-1 each have immunoprotective effects in the ageing spleen. Vilon and R-1 are described as activating T-helper cells, while Timogen and Crystagen activate B-cells; Crystagen is reported not to drive cell renewal in the ageing spleen.[1]

Wikipedia's article on the related peptide epitalon notes that most research on Khavinson-group peptides comes from the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and that independent replication is not reported, with the page flagged for relying heavily on primary sources.[2]

chain: Peptide reported to activate B-cells in ageing spleen
angle.text: Crystagen is described as a bioregulator for immune function in ageing. Any effect on appearance is a claimed, indirect extension of general anti-ageing aims, and no human appearance outcomes have been reported.

infobox: Research peptide; no established clinical use

paras: Crystagen belongs to a family of very short peptides, including Vilon, Timogen and Epitalon, that researchers associated with Khavinson propose as regulators of tissue function and ageing. It is a tripeptide made of threonine, lysine and glutamic acid.[1]

Epitalon, a four-amino-acid member of the family, was identified as the likely active component of epithalamin, a bovine pineal extract, and its human studies are small, with reports of 79 and 266 participants.[2]

A 2014 paper in Advances in Gerontology reports that Vilon and R-1 act on T-helper cells, Timogen activates B-cells by decreasing apoptosis and increasing spleen cell proliferation, and Crystagen also activates B-cells without causing cell renewal in the ageing spleen.[1]
No studies found in humans. The only material is a laboratory-level report on spleen immune cells in the context of ageing.[1]
Crystagen is rarely discussed on appearance forums; it appears mainly in lists of Khavinson bioregulators tied to the immune-system claims made for that peptide family.

timeline.event: Paper reports immunoprotective effects of Vilon, Timogen, Crystagen and R-1 peptides in the ageing spleen.[1]

refs.title: Molecular aspects of immunoprotective activity of peptides in spleen during the ageing process
